newsitem.title: UK: British scientists target cancer gene with drug.
newsitem.headline: British scientists target cancer gene with drug.

text.p: British scientists said on Thursday they were developing a drug that overcomes a defect blamed in many cases of cancer.
They are targeting a protein, mdm-2, they say prevents the p53 gene from working properly. An antibody can be used to block the protein, they reported in the journal Oncogene.
David Wynford-Thomas and David Lane of the Cancer Research Campaign said their research could help sufferers of breast, thyroid and malignant skin cancer.
The p53 gene, also known as one of the tumour suppressor genes, has been found to be mutated in many cancer sufferers.

Normally it switches on a process known as apoptosis, when damaged cells destroy themselves before they start the out-of-control growth that marks cancer. It is a favourite target of researchers trying to develop gene therapy -- which would cure by replacing faulty genes with properly functioning ones. But Wynford-Thomas and Lane are taking a different route.
They first found that the p53 protein, which the p53 gene programmes for, was not faulty in thyroid cancer, but merely blocked from working by the mdm-2 protein.

"We already know that the mdm-2 (protein) can be knocked out by an antibody and that this then stops the cancer cells from growing," Wynford-Thomas, who works at the University of Dundee, said in a statement.

He said his team was developing a drug that would imitate the antibody and restore p53's function as a tumour suppressor. "It is likely that the drug will not have any of the unpleasant side-effects that are part and parcel of conventional chemotherapy," Wynford-Thomas said.
"This research opens up a new direction in the search for really effective therapies, although it is only in the early stages of drug development."
